paras: The attempted lynching of Neely Zimmerman and George Williams took place in Council Bluffs, Iowa, on the night of 28-29 December 1903, when a crowd broke down the door of the Pottawattamie county jail to seize two Black men charged with robbing and attempting to assault two white women. Deputy sheriffs turned the crowd back, Congressman Walter I. Smith persuaded it to disperse, and the men were moved to the penitentiary at Fort Madison the next day. The wire carried it nationally as a lynching narrowly averted, and Black papers praised Smith for upholding the law.

Zimmerman and Williams, who admitted his real name was Burk, were charged with robbing Mrs. Mary Starks and her daughter, Mrs. Harry Sanders, after the women left a streetcar late on Christmas night, and with attempting to assault them. Police arrested them on 27 December, and Mrs. Sanders identified both men. A crowd rushed the patrol wagon as they were taken away, and onlookers said the men "ought to be lynched", so they were sent to the county jail. According to a wire report, four similar assaults in a week had "wrought up the working people of the city".

At their arraignment on 28 December both men denied the charge, and Sanders's husband struck Zimmerman in the face as he was led out. That evening several hundred men and boys gathered at the jail, jeered the police and jostled Mayor Morgan when he urged them to go home. The Associated Press put the crowd at 500, growing to at least 1,000, and said it demanded the prisoners.

Men brought a rail from the railroad yards and broke in the front door, just after midnight according to the wire or about 1:30 according to the Omaha Bee. Deputy sheriffs with drawn revolvers ordered the intruders back and cleared the jail. Smith persuaded George Sanders, husband of one of the women, to go home and promised the crowd a fair trial; police arrested Nate Bethers and a man named Knight for inciting riot, and the crowd melted away. Governor Cummins had ordered out the militia, which the Associated Press said arrived after the crowd had gone.

On 29 December Sheriff Cousins heard of an organized plan for a second attempt, and the men waived preliminary examination before Judge Wheeler, who ordered their removal. They were taken that evening by train to Fort Madison, Zimmerman exclaiming as they left, "Now we will be killed sure." County authorities said friends of W. C. Rogers, a jail prisoner charged with murder, had urged the attack in hope of freeing him, and a third man, Charles Stevenson, was arrested for inciting riot.

Prison officials reportedly recognized both prisoners as former inmates. A local paper reported in February 1904 that the two had been sentenced to 25 years each; no report of the trial itself appears in the coverage.

The wire story ran on 29 and 30 December from Washington and Providence to Butte, under headlines such as "IOWANS SEEK TO LYNCH TWO NEGRO PRISONERS" and "SAVED NEGROES." It took the charge for granted: the Washington Times wrote that but for Smith both men "would have paid the penalty of their crime with their lives." The Omaha Bee's local report, "CROWD ONLY LACKS LEADER", concluded that only the lack of a leader had prevented a lynching. Iowa papers then turned to the prisoners' records: "THEY'RE BAD ONES." and "ZIMMERMAN'S BAD RECORD."

Among Black papers, the Iowa State Bystander, under "The Council Bluffs Attempted Disgrace", wrote that Iowa was saved "from the infamous disgrace of lynching, that is common in our southern states," though it called the accused "fiends". The St. Paul Appeal thanked Smith for dispersing "the thieves" at the jail and demanded that punishment be legal. The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the removal dispatch as "BAD NEGROES.", and the Richmond Planet's digest stated as fact that the men had assaulted the women.

Accounts differ on the crowd's size and on what ended the siege: the wire credited Smith's appeal through Sanders and news of the militia, while the Omaha Bee also credited the deputies and the arrests. The claim that Rogers's friends drove the attack comes only from county authorities.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Neely Zimmerman and George Williams
bases: A crowd broke into the Council Bluffs jail to lynch two Black prisoners and was turned back; no one was killed (A4, A9, A16).

A crowd of hundreds acting on a crime accusation tried to take the men from jail (A4, A9), but both survived and were moved to Fort Madison (A15, A16), so this is an attempted lynching, not a lynching.
The local Omaha Bee (A4), the Associated Press wire (A9) and the Iowa State Bystander (A26) independently agree that a crowd broke the jail door and was dispersed.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee (local Council Bluffs page)
accounts.gist: A crowd of curious onlookers lacking a leader broke the door about 1:30; deputies with drawn revolvers cleared the jail, Smith and Tinley spoke, two arrests thinned the crowd, and the militia was called on a rumor of a second crowd.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: A mob of 500 to 1,000 battered the door with railroad iron just after midnight; Smith persuaded Sanders to go home and the crowd left, before the militia arrived (or on news that it was coming).

accounts.label: County authorities
accounts.gist: The attack was prompted in large part by friends of W. C. Rogers, a murder defendant in the jail, who hoped to free him.

accounts.label: Iowa State Bystander
accounts.gist: The crowd battered down the door and began on the inner doors before Smith's appeal; Iowa was spared the disgrace of a lynching.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'IOWANS SEEK TO LYNCH TWO NEGRO PRISONERS' and 'MOB BATTERS AT DOORS OF BASTILE' reported the mob critically, but the Washington Times wrote that the men would have 'paid the penalty of their crime', treating the charge as proven.
The Omaha Bee's local report, 'CROWD ONLY LACKS LEADER', described a mostly curious crowd and credited the deputies and Smith.
Follow-ups headed 'THEY'RE BAD ONES.' and 'ZIMMERMAN'S BAD RECORD.' dwelt on the men's prior prison terms rather than the mob.
The Missouri Valley Times closed its sentencing brief with 'That is better than mob law.'
The Iowa State Bystander headed its item 'The Council Bluffs Attempted Disgrace' and called lynching a southern 'infamous disgrace', while calling the accused 'fiends'.
The St. Paul Appeal thanked Smith for dispersing 'the thieves' at the jail and insisted punishment be administered legally.
The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the removal wire under 'BAD NEGROES.'; the Richmond Planet's digest stated as fact that the men 'criminally assaulted two white women'.

info: Arrest Sunday 27 December 1903; mob attack on the county jail the night of Monday 28 December into the early hours of 29 December; removal to Fort Madison on the afternoon/evening of 29 December
Two Black men: Neely (Neeley, Nelly) Zimmerman and George Williams, alias Burk/Burke (reported also as George Burk, George Burke)
Charged with robbing and attempting to criminally assault Mrs. Mary Starks (Sparks, Stark) and her daughter Mrs. Sanders on Christmas night, 25 December 1903; both denied the charge

A crowd of men and boys; three men (Nate Bethers, John or George Knight, Charles 'Dutch' Stevenson) arrested on charges of inciting riot; county authorities said friends of jail prisoner W. C. Rogers urged the attack
The two men were reported sentenced to 25 years each in the penitentiary about 17 February 1904
